catalog_quote: From the above we may deduce that the following rules apply for stress: (1) Stress always occurs on the grammatical root. (2) Stress may occur on any of the last three syllables of the root. Observations: 1) If the stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable of the root, the final syllable is always /?u/ or /tu/. There is only one exception to this rule. The sequence voiceless plosive followed by /u/ (VLPu) may then be called an extrametrical syllable, as it is not counted in the positioning of the stress. We can thus rewrite rule 2, above, to say that stress may occur on the last two syllables of the root, but that a syllable type VLPu when it occurs root finally does not count in reckoning the syllable position. 2) It is not predictable whether stress will occur on the penultimate or the final syllable of the root, although it is more common on the penultimate syllable. audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated pages (WILC 7, pp. 60-61) in the page-image PDF we hold via its scanned. The deciding source is the only dedicated phonology of Dobel, written by the language's principal fieldworkers, and the same author's later PL-503 chapter (2000, held) independently restates the analysis with a quantitative root count (20% final stress in 1,920 polysyllabic roots), confirming 'lexical (contrastive) stress in a right-edge root window with VLPu extrametricality, affixes never stressed'. StressTyp2 codes the language identically from the same source. No better or newer description exists in Glottolog's bibliography or CrossRef. Two optional refinements, neither changing classification lexical: (a) the secondary-stress rule could cite Hughes 2000 p. 134, which mentions secondary stress two syllables before the primary (so 'no secondary stress described' is slightly too strong); (b) the primary-stress rule could add Hugh

tone.quote: The eastern Indonesian languages Manggarai, Ngad'a, Lamaholot, Woisika, Leti, Selaru, Wolio are classified as "no fixed stress" in the StressTyp database because they avoid stressed schwa and thus show "variability". However, all of them are otherwise described as displaying penultimate stress and fall squarely within the Eastern Prototype. Even Dobel, a rare example of an eastern Indonesian languages that shows phonemic/lexical stress, as shown in (1), is described as having penultimate stress as its basic pattern (Hughes 2000:135). (1) Dobel (Hughes 2000:135) /da-ˈtabay/ 'they carry (on shoulder)' /ˈʔala-y/ 'its/his skin' /da-taˈbay/ 'they hit' /ʔaˈla-y/ 'kind of lemon'
